Commentary.Commentary: We are back for the all-important chase! One last time in this ICC Women's World Cup 2025, as the crowd roars with history beckoning. India Women players are in a huddle, where Harmanpreet Kaur is giving them a last-minute pep talk before they spread out and take their respective field positions. Laura Wolvaardt, after playing the knock of her life in the semi-final against England, walks out to open for South Africa Women, alongside in-form Tazmin Brits. Renuka Singh Thakur will start proceedings with the ball. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

This hasn’t been as easy a track to bat on as the one for the India-Australia semifinal. As the ball got older, the cutters began to grip and hold up on the surface, though it could skid onto the bat in the second innings with the possibility of dew. And remember, with the start delayed by two hours, the dew could settle in earlier, something that could have a major say in how this chase unfolds. South Africa have chased four times so far in this World Cup and have been successful on every occasion. That said, the pressure of a World Cup final is a different ball game, especially when you are chasing your first-ever World Cup title. It is all set up for an intriguing chase. Stay tuned!

South Africa's Nonkululeko Mlaba is up for a chat. She admits that the bowlers didn’t start well, but was pleased with how they pulled things back. She says the plan was to keep things simple and bowl stump to stump. Speaking about her own performance, Mlaba also notes that bowling slower through the air worked in her favour on this surface. She acknowledges that it’s a high-scoring ground but expresses full confidence in the team’s ability to chase it down.

From there, it was an arm wrestle. Whenever India looked to build a partnership, South Africa hit back to keep them in check. Deepti Sharma held one end together, and towards the end, Richa Ghosh played her part in trying to push India past 300. However, Ghosh fell in the penultimate over, and Nadine De Klerk nailed the final over, conceding just six runs. Only 12 runs came off the last two overs, and that could very well prove to be the difference by the end of the night. On a night when Marizanne Kapp went wicketless, Nadine De Klerk, Ayabonga Khaka, and Nonkululeko Mlaba stepped up admirably to ensure India didn’t run away with the game. It was all about how they adapted, keeping the stumps in play and using clever variations, particularly from De Klerk.

Having lost the toss, a stiff challenge awaited upfront for the two Indian openers, Shafali Verma and Smriti Mandhana, against the Proteas’ new-ball attack on a surface that was expected to have something in it early on following the rain before the game. Ayabonga Khaka found a fair bit of swing but lacked control, while Marizanne Kapp couldn’t find much movement at all. That allowed India to get off to a commanding start, forcing Nonkululeko Mlaba and Nadine De Klerk to be introduced earlier than usual. The duo managed to stitch together a quiet phase, but it didn’t bring about a breakthrough. Mandhana eventually fell, but Verma carried on and enjoyed a slice of luck when she was dropped on 56 by Anneke Bosch. She went on to make 87 before the Proteas struck twice in quick succession, with Khaka’s double blow pushing India into rebuild mode.

Excellent final over from Nadine De Klerk! South Africa have managed to keep India under 300 and deny them the psychological edge at the halfway mark. Laura Wolvaardt will be pleased with how her side pulled things back, especially after the start India had. The Women in Blue, meanwhile, will feel they could have gotten more, but runs on the board in a final are always precious and 298 is, after all, the second-highest total in a Women's World Cup final.

OUT! DEEPTI SHARMA IS RUN OUT! A full toss on middle and off, and Radha swings hard, aiming for the stands but loses all shape in the process and the bat slips out of her hands as well. The ball is sliced off the outer half of the bat, and rolls past backward point. Both batters initially commit to the second run, but Deepti is a bit slow to turn around to cross over. The fielder, Chloe Tryon, spots Deepti way out of the crease and throws it to the keeper. Sinalo Jafta has ample time to collect the ball and whip the bails off. Since the batters didn't cross each other, it is Deepti who has to walk back. Just six singles off the final over. INDIA WOMEN FINISH ON 298/7

A bit of hesitation between the two batters for the single before they decide against it. Nadine De Klerk was quick to get to the ball with a slide to her right.

Commentary.Commentary: Wow, the atmosphere at the DY Patil Stadium is electric. Both anthems are sung with pride and emotion and it is now time for the Grand Finale to get underway. We are starting a couple of hours late, but NO OVERS ARE LOST. Needless to say, not a single empty seat in the stadium. Now then, the Proteas spread out of the huddle to take their respective positions on the field. Shafali Verma accompanies Smriti Mandhana to open for India. And Marizanne Kapp has the new ball, raring to go with two slips in waiting. Smriti to face. Here we go...

The flags are unveiled in the middle as both sets of players, followed by the match officials, walk out for the national anthems. It will be South Africa's first, which will be sung by the famous pop singer from South Africa, Tarryn Lamb. And now, it will be the famous Indian singer, Sunidhi Chauhan, to sing the national anthem of India.

India's captain, Harmanpreet Kaur, says that they would have bowled first as well, given the overhead conditions. Believes that batting first will help them bat freely and hopes to put a decent total on the board. Reckons that the wicket is a bit sticky due to the rain. Adds that she does not expect the surface to do much after the first few overs because of the possibility of the ball getting wet in the outfield. Informs that they are unchanged for the final. Shares that they had 2 days to recover after the semifinal and that they are looking forward to this clash.

The captain of South Africa, Laura Wolvaardt, says it is a nice chasing ground and there is a possibility of dew coming in later as well. Adds that the wicket looks nice and reckons that it may stick a bit with the rain around. Shares that they haven't played a game at this venue yet, but also details that they have been good in the Powerplay so far. Informs that they are going unchanged for the finale. Ends by saying this is a great opportunity for them in front of such a crowd, and they are taking the positives in the game.

South Africa Women (Unchanged Playing XI) - Laura Wolvaardt (C), Tazmin Brits, Anneke Bosch, Sune Luus, Marizanne Kapp, Sinalo Jafta (WK), Chloe Tryon, Annerie Dercksen, Nadine De Klerk, Ayabonga Khaka, Nonkululeko Mlaba.

India Women (Unchanged Playing XI) - Shafali Verma, Smriti Mandhana, Jemimah Rodrigues, Harmanpreet Kaur (C), Deepti Sharma, Richa Ghosh (WK), Amanjot Kaur, Radha Yadav, Kranti Gaud, Sree Charani, Renuka Singh Thakur.
TOSS - Laura Wolvaardt calls it correctly and South Africa have elected to BOWL first.
Interestingly, both teams have had identical luck at the toss, having won it only once in the eight games so far. They will be hoping that Lady Luck shines on them today.

UPDATE - 4.18 pm IST (10.48 am GMT) - The rain has stopped, and the match officials have called on the two captains. Smriti Mandhana walks up for the meeting in place of Harmanpreet Kaur. The Indian players have also returned to the park after briefly heading back to the dugout during that short drizzle. It looks like we are on course for the flip of the coin at 4.32 pm IST (11.02 am GMT), with the first ball scheduled for 5 pm IST (11.30 am GMT). No overs have been lost yet.

UPDATE - 4.09 pm IST (10.39 am GMT) - Oopsie! The rain is back. Just when we were getting our hopes up, it has returned to dampen our spirits once again. The ground staff rush back into action as the covers make their way onto the square. It’s just a light drizzle for now, but enough for the centre cover to be put on.

UPDATE - 4.05 pm IST (10.35 am GMT) - There you go! Toss to take place at 4.32 pm IST (11.02 am GMT) with the summit clash set to begin at 5 pm IST (11.30 am GMT). Since we have two hours of buffer time for the final, no overs have been lost yet, but any further delays could see overs being reduced. Harmanpreet Kaur and Indian head coach Amol Muzumdar are currently having a close look at the deck.

UPDATE - 4.02 pm IST (10.32 am GMT) - The match officials are making their way out for an inspection as the Super Sopper buzzes across the outfield. The pitch has been uncovered and is now being rolled. The two captains have been called over by the on-field umpires, who are relaying their observations. Stick around. We could have an update soon regarding the revised timings.

UPDATE - 3.54 pm IST (10.24 am GMT) - Good news! The rain has subsided. The covers are coming off, and that has been greeted by a loud cheer from the crowd. The skies have cleared up a bit, with the sun trying to peek through the clouds. The ground staff will now have to deal with the puddles, which could take some time, but the rain has stopped, and that’s the most important thing. Fingers crossed that the weather holds for the rest of the day.

UPDATE - 3.46 pm IST (10.16 am GMT) - Still raining steadily in Navi Mumbai, unfortunately. However, we are hearing that the cut-off time for a 20-over per side contest is 9.08 pm IST (3.38 pm GMT). And if play doesn't commence by this cut-off time, the reserve day will come into effect.

UPDATE - 3.27 pm IST (9.57 am GMT) - The rain appears to have eased up a bit, if not stopped completely. Live visuals still show the umpires huddled near the covers in deep conversation with the ground staff, though crucially, their umbrellas remain raised above them. There are numerous puddles formed across the field. Hence, even when the rain stops, the ground staff will need considerable time to clear them up.

UPDATE - 3.01 pm IST (9.31 am GMT) - It is absolutely pelting down at the moment. We were hoping to have the toss around this time, but the rain gods seem to have other plans. With this latest spell, and judging by the intensity of the downpour, it looks like it will be a while before we get any action.

UPDATE - 2.46 pm IST (9.16 am GMT) - Well, the rain has picked up, and more covers will have to be brought on. We are hearing that there is a two-hour buffer in place for the final before we start losing overs, as compared to the one-hour window available during the league stage.

UPDATE - 2.37 pm IST (9.07 am GMT) - Oh no! The rain has returned, and the covers are going back on. It’s just a light drizzle at the moment, with the players still continuing their warm-ups. For now, only the centre cover is on.

UPDATE - 2.29 pm IST (8.59 am GMT) - Right then, the pitch has been uncovered, and the official word is in. Toss to take place at 3 pm IST (9.30 am GMT) with the first ball of the final to be bowled at 3.30 pm IST (10 am GMT).

UPDATE - 2.17 pm IST (8.47 am GMT) - It has stopped raining, and the conditions have brightened up considerably. With around 15 minutes left for the scheduled toss, the flip of the coin will likely be delayed. No official word just yet, so we will have to wait and see. The covers are coming off, but a few puddles have been spotted, which will need some attention from the ground staff.

UPDATE - 2.09 pm IST (8.39 am GMT) - Unfortunately, rain has descended over the Dr. DY Patil Stadium, and the covers are on at the moment. It has been raining steadily for more than half an hour now, which certainly puts a damper on the occasion. However, with a reserve day in place, there is no immediate cause for concern. Looking at the radar, it doesn’t appear that we will need it, as the weather is expected to clear in the next couple of hours.

The stage is set for the grand finale at the Dr. DY Patil Sports Academy in Navi Mumbai! This is the same venue where Kaur and Jemimah scripted that record chase against Australia in the semifinals, showing how good this pitch can be for batting. The surface might offer a bit to the spinners early on, as we saw in the last match. With a packed house and billions watching, India enter as slight favourites, but two years ago, the Indian men were in a similar position here at home, only to face heartbreak against Australia. The Women in Blue will hope history doesn’t repeat itself, but South African Women have the belief and balance to flip the script and lift their first-ever World Cup.

Now, shifting focus to South Africa - a team that’s turning finals into a habit. After reaching the T20 World Cup final in 2023 and 2024, they’re back on the grand stage once again. Their campaign has been impressive, with only two slip-ups in the group stage where they were bowled out for 69 against England - the only real blemish in an otherwise dominant run. Their semifinal against England was nothing short of spectacular - Laura Wolvaardt’s breathtaking 169 and Marizanne Kapp’s five-wicket haul perfectly summed up their class and composure. Add to that the brilliance of Tazmin Brits, who’s in red-hot form with five centuries this year - a record matched only by India’s Smriti Mandhana, and both now have the chance to go one better in the biggest game of their careers. Ayabonga Khaka and Nonkululeko Mlaba have been consistent with the ball, while the all-round impact of Chloe Tryon and Nadine De Klerk, especially the latter’s match-winning 84 off 54 against India earlier, gives them great balance. They fell short in the T20 World Cup final on a couple of occasions, but this time, they’ll be desperate to rewrite history and bring home a maiden World Cup title.

Let’s begin with India. They kicked off their World Cup campaign strongly with a couple of solid wins, but then stumbled with three consecutive losses, starting against South Africa, where they just couldn’t close out games despite competing well. Consistency, particularly with the ball and in the field, seemed to be the missing link. But when they needed someone to step up, Smriti Mandhana and Pratika Rawal delivered with twin centuries against New Zealand to seal a semifinal berth. What followed was pure magic - up against defending champions Australia, it seemed another heartbreak was on the cards, until skipper Harmanpreet Kaur and Jemmimah Rodrigues turned it around. Rodrigues’ sensational, unbeaten 127 lit up the night and filled a billion hearts with pride. Alongside them, Deepti Sharma, Richa Ghosh, and Kranti Gaud have all played key roles, but now, it’s time for one final push to turn dreams into reality.

And here we are - the grand finale! After 30 enthralling encounters that had it all - edge-of-the-seat thrillers, rain playing its part, and emotional farewells to legends - it all comes down to this final showdown. A very warm welcome to our coverage of the much-anticipated ICC Women’s World Cup 2025 final. Two teams brimming with talent, resilience, and sheer determination face off for ultimate glory. It’s India taking on South Africa in what promises to be a riveting contest, and the best part, we’re guaranteed to witness a new champion being crowned today!

The curtain is set to fall on a captivating ICC Women's Cricket World Cup 2025 with a final that guarantees history will be made. Hosts India Women will lock horns with South Africa Women at the Dr. DY Patil Sports Academy in Navi Mumbai in a showdown where the winner will be crowned World Champions for the very first time. Both teams have navigated a challenging tournament, slaying cricketing giants in the process, to reach this ultimate summit. India overcame the mighty defending champions Australia in a thrilling semi-final, while South Africa dismantled the highly-fancied England side in a dominant performance to secure their maiden Women's World Cup final berth. For India, this final is a shot at redemption after finishing as runners-up in 2005 and 2017. Their journey has been a blend of resilience and explosive performances. The historic semi-final chase of 339 against Australia, orchestrated by a brilliant, anchoring century from Jemimah Rodrigues, and an attacking 89 from Harmanpreet Kaur, has injected immense belief into the squad. India has the added advantage of familiarity with the venue, having remained undefeated at the DY Patil Stadium this tournament. Their batting depth has held up under pressure, while their spinning contingent, led by Deepti Sharma and Sree Charani, has been instrumental in controlling the middle overs. On the other hand, South Africa's journey has been a true testament to grit and peaking at the right time. The Proteas shrugged off a heavy opening defeat to England to build momentum, culminating in a commanding 125-run victory over the same opponent in the semi-final. Skipper Laura Wolvaardt has led from the front, becoming the tournament's leading run-scorer with 470 runs. This is their first-ever World Cup final in the 50-over format, making it an emotionally charged encounter for the whole nation. A notable challenge for South Africa is the venue, as they have not played at the DY Patil Stadium yet in this tournament. However, their team spirit and the confidence gained from their semi-final demolition of England will fuel their campaign. The battle between India's in-form top-order and South Africa's pace spearheads like Marizanne Kapp and Ayabonga Khaka, as well as the mid-innings contest between the spin bowling of both teams, will be fascinating to watch. The DY Patil Stadium pitch is renowned as a batting-friendly track, as proven by India's record-breaking chase in the semi-final. While early overcast conditions might offer something to the seamers, a high-scoring contest is expected. The team that manages to control the powerplay phases, both with bat and ball, is likely to hold the upper hand. Who are you backing to lift their maiden Women's World Cup trophy?
